claim: 91 ZAD-ZNF genes are distributed across Chromosomes 2, 3, and X in D. melanogaster.
source: We found 91 ZAD-ZNF genes distributed across Chromosomes 2, 3, and X.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the manuscript reporting the number and chromosomal distribution of ZAD-ZNF genes identified in D. melanogaster.

claim: 37 ZAD-ZNF genes occur in 13 gene clusters containing two or more tandemly-arrayed ZAD-ZNF genes.
source: 37 ZAD-ZNF genes occur in 13 gene clusters, containing two or more tandemly-arrayed ZAD-ZNF genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the clustering pattern of ZAD-ZNF genes based on genomic analysis.

claim: Seven ZAD-ZNF genes (CG3032, CG4318, CG9215, CG44002, CG17361, CG7963, CG17359) lack introns found in their closest relatives and likely arose via retrotransposition.
source: In contrast, seven ZAD-ZNF genes (CG3032, CG4318, CG9215, CG44002, CG17361, CG7963, CG17359) lack introns found in their closest relatives; we infer that these genes were likely born via retrotransposition.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of genes (lack of introns) and inference about their evolutionary origin.

claim: ZAD-containing proteins have an average of six C2H2 domains.
source: We found that ZAD-containing proteins have an average of six C2H2 domains.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the average number of C2H2 domains based on domain analysis.

claim: Some ZAD-containing proteins have no C2H2 domains at all (dlip, dbr, CG15435, CG31109, CG31457).
source: However, some ZAD-containing proteins have no C2H2 domains at all (dlip, dbr, CG15435, CG31109, CG31457), whereas others contain up to 23 C2H2 domains (CG11902).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the variation in C2H2 domain numbers based on domain analysis.

claim: Some ZAD-containing proteins contain up to 23 C2H2 domains (CG11902).
source: However, some ZAD-containing proteins have no C2H2 domains at all (dlip, dbr, CG15435, CG31109, CG31457), whereas others contain up to 23 C2H2 domains (CG11902).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the maximum number of C2H2 domains found in a ZAD-containing protein.

claim: 13 ZAD-ZNF proteins possess another N-terminal domain in addition to the ZAD.
source: In addition to the ZAD in the N-terminus, 13 ZAD-ZNF proteins possess another N-terminal domain, such as a Sodium-Calcium exchanger domain (CG12391) or ASF1 histone chaperone domain (CG10321).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the presence of additional N-terminal domains based on domain analysis.

claim: The D. persimilis genome encodes 130 ZAD-ZNF genes.
source: For example, we found that the D. persimilis genome encodes 130 ZAD-ZNF genes whereas the D. willistoni genome encodes only 75 ZAD-ZNF genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of ZAD-ZNF genes in D. persimilis based on genome analysis, with reference to supplementary data and Figure 1.

claim: The D. willistoni genome encodes only 75 ZAD-ZNF genes.
source: For example, we found that the D. persimilis genome encodes 130 ZAD-ZNF genes whereas the D. willistoni genome encodes only 75 ZAD-ZNF genes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of ZAD-ZNF genes in D. willistoni based on genome analysis, with reference to supplementary data and Figure 1.

claim: 74 of 91 D. melanogaster ZAD-ZNF genes arose in or prior to the common ancestor of all Drosophila species, 40 million years ago.
source: We found that 74 of 91 D. melanogaster ZAD-ZNF genes arose in or prior to the common ancestor of all Drosophila species, 40 million years ago.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the evolutionary age of ZAD-ZNF genes based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: 61 of 74 ancient ZAD-ZNF genes have been preserved over Drosophila evolution.
source: Of these 74 ZAD-ZNF genes, 61 have been preserved over Drosophila evolution, whereas 13 have been lost in at least one lineage or species.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the retention pattern of ancient ZAD-ZNF genes based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: 13 ancient ZAD-ZNF genes have been lost in at least one lineage or species.
source: Of these 74 ZAD-ZNF genes, 61 have been preserved over Drosophila evolution, whereas 13 have been lost in at least one lineage or species.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the loss pattern of ancient ZAD-ZNF genes based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: 17 ZAD-ZNF genes arose via gene duplication after the last common ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
source: We estimate that 17 ZAD-ZNF genes arose via gene duplication after the last common ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. virilis.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of recently duplicated ZAD-ZNF genes based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: At least 3 ZAD-ZNF genes found in D. melanogaster (CG4318, CG17612, neu2) originated via gene duplication less than 10 million years ago.
source: At least 3 ZAD-ZNF genes found in D. melanogaster (CG4318, CG17612, neu2) originated via gene duplication less than 10 million years ago.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the very recent origin of specific ZAD-ZNF genes based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: 85 of 91 D. melanogaster ZAD-ZNF genes have associated phenotypic outcomes.
source: Indeed, 85 of 91 D. melanogaster ZAD-ZNF genes have associated phenotypic outcomes (summarized in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the availability of phenotypic data for ZAD-ZNF genes.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of 22 ZAD-ZNF genes showed complete lethality or sterility in D. melanogaster.
source: Of these, knockdown or knockout of 22 ZAD-ZNF genes showed complete lethality or sterility in D. melanogaster, whereas the other 63 were determined not to be essential.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of essential ZAD-ZNF genes based on phenotypic data.

claim: 63 ZAD-ZNF genes were determined not to be essential.
source: Of these, knockdown or knockout of 22 ZAD-ZNF genes showed complete lethality or sterility in D. melanogaster, whereas the other 63 were determined not to be essential.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of non-essential ZAD-ZNF genes based on phenotypic data.

claim: 14 of 61 ZAD-ZNF genes with orthologs retained in all 12 annotated Drosophila species' genomes are essential for either fertility or viability in D. melanogaster.
source: Of the 61 ZAD-ZNF genes with orthologs retained in all 12 annotated Drosophila species' genomes, we found that 14 are essential for either fertility or viability in D. melanogaster, whereas 42 genes are not (five genes have no phenotypic data available).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the essentiality of conserved ZAD-ZNF genes based on phenotypic data.

claim: 42 of 61 conserved ZAD-ZNF genes are not essential.
source: Of the 61 ZAD-ZNF genes with orthologs retained in all 12 annotated Drosophila species' genomes, we found that 14 are essential for either fertility or viability in D. melanogaster, whereas 42 genes are not (five genes have no phenotypic data available).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the non-essentiality of conserved ZAD-ZNF genes based on phenotypic data.

claim: 8 of 30 ZAD-ZNF genes not universally conserved in Drosophila species are essential.
source: In comparison, we found that 8 of the 30 genes not universally conserved in Drosophila species are essential, whereas 21 are not (one has no phenotypic data available).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the essentiality of non-conserved ZAD-ZNF genes based on phenotypic data.

claim: 21 of 30 non-conserved ZAD-ZNF genes are not essential.
source: In comparison, we found that 8 of the 30 genes not universally conserved in Drosophila species are essential, whereas 21 are not (one has no phenotypic data available).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the non-essentiality of non-conserved ZAD-ZNF genes based on phenotypic data.

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes not globally retained over Drosophila evolution are just as likely to encode a necessary function in D. melanogaster as genes that have been strictly maintained over 40 million years of Drosophila evolution (p=0.8).
source: Thus, somewhat surprisingly, we find that genes not globally retained over Drosophila evolution are just as likely to encode a necessary function in D. melanogaster as genes that have been strictly maintained over 40 million years of Drosophila evolution (8:21 versus 14:42, p=0.8, two-tailed Fisher's exact test) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting a statistical comparison of essentiality between conserved and non-conserved genes.

claim: 12 out of 90 ZAD-ZNF genes show evidence for recent adaptive evolution based on McDonald-Kreitman test.
source: We found that 12 out of the remaining 90 ZAD-ZNFs show evidence for recent adaptive evolution, i.e., have an excess of fixed non-synonymous changes (Dn) (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of positively selected ZAD-ZNF genes based on McDonald-Kreitman test.

claim: 5 out of 12 positively selected ZAD-ZNF genes showed evidence of positive selection with polarized McDonald-Kreitman test using D. yakuba as an outgroup.
source: Using D. yakuba as an outgroup species, we also polarized fixed differences between D. melanogaster and D. simulans to assess whether the lineage leading to D. melanogaster showed evidence of positive selection in these 12 ZAD-ZNF genes. We found that 5 out of 12 genes showed evidence of positive selection with this polarized McDonald-Kreitman test (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of genes showing positive selection in the polarized test.

claim: The linker domain has evolved under positive selection in six ZAD-ZNF genes.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the linker domain has evolved under positive selection in six ZAD-ZNF genes.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting domain-specific positive selection based on McDonald-Kreitman test.

claim: One gene (CG7386) showed signatures of adaptive evolution in its ZAD domain.
source: One gene (CG7386) showed signatures of adaptive evolution in its ZAD domain, whereas three genes (CG2712, CG7386, CG10321) showed evidence of adaptive evolution in the ZNF domain.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting domain-specific positive selection based on McDonald-Kreitman test.

claim: Three genes (CG2712, CG7386, CG10321) showed evidence of adaptive evolution in the ZNF domain.
source: One gene (CG7386) showed signatures of adaptive evolution in its ZAD domain, whereas three genes (CG2712, CG7386, CG10321) showed evidence of adaptive evolution in the ZNF domain.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting domain-specific positive selection based on McDonald-Kreitman test.

claim: 8 of 12 ZAD-ZNF genes that have evolved under positive selection are essential.
source: Intriguingly, we found that 8 of 12 ZAD-ZNF genes that have evolved under positive selection are essential, whereas only 14 of the remaining 73 genes that have been phenotypically assayed are essential (six have no phenotypic data available).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the essentiality of positively selected ZAD-ZNF genes.

claim: 14 of 73 ZAD-ZNF genes not under positive selection are essential.
source: Intriguingly, we found that 8 of 12 ZAD-ZNF genes that have evolved under positive selection are essential, whereas only 14 of the remaining 73 genes that have been phenotypically assayed are essential (six have no phenotypic data available).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the essentiality of non-positively selected ZAD-ZNF genes.

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes that are subject to positive selection are more likely to be essential for viability or fertility (p=0.0016).
source: Thus, contrary to the dogma, we find that ZAD-ZNF genes that are subject to positive selection are more likely to be essential for viability or fertility (8:4 versus 14:59, two-tailed Fisher's exact test, p=0.0016) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting a statistically significant correlation between positive selection and essentiality.

claim: The Oddjob-Nicknack cluster contains five ZAD-ZNF genes on chromosome 3 of D. melanogaster.
source: To further investigate the biological basis for the correlation between positive selection and gene essentiality, we decided to focus on one cluster of ZAD-ZNF genes on chromosome 3 of D. melanogaster (Figure 2A). This cluster of five genes contains two of the eight positively-selected, essential genes in D. melanogaster: Oddjob (Odj, CG7357) and CG17802
evidence: This is a direct statement describing the composition of the Oddjob-Nicknack cluster, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Oddjob (Odj, CG7357) and CG17802 (Nicknack) are two of the eight positively-selected, essential genes in D. melanogaster.
source: This cluster of five genes contains two of the eight positively-selected, essential genes in D. melanogaster: Oddjob (Odj, CG7357) and CG17802; both also show evidence of positive selection in the polarized McDonald-Kreitman test (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement identifying two positively selected essential genes in the cluster.

claim: Both Oddjob and Nicknack show evidence of positive selection in the polarized McDonald-Kreitman test.
source: This cluster of five genes contains two of the eight positively-selected, essential genes in D. melanogaster: Oddjob (Odj, CG7357) and CG17802; both also show evidence of positive selection in the polarized McDonald-Kreitman test (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting positive selection in both genes using the polarized test.

claim: The Oddjob protein interacts with Heterochromatin Protein 1a (HP1a).
source: The Oddjob protein interacts with Heterochromatin Protein 1a (HP1a), dynamically localizes to heterochromatin, and is required for heterochromatin-mediated gene silencing, or position-effect variegation (Swenson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study that characterized Oddjob protein function.

claim: Oddjob dynamically localizes to heterochromatin.
source: The Oddjob protein interacts with Heterochromatin Protein 1a (HP1a), dynamically localizes to heterochromatin, and is required for heterochromatin-mediated gene silencing, or position-effect variegation (Swenson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study that characterized Oddjob protein localization.

claim: Oddjob is required for heterochromatin-mediated gene silencing, or position-effect variegation.
source: The Oddjob protein interacts with Heterochromatin Protein 1a (HP1a), dynamically localizes to heterochromatin, and is required for heterochromatin-mediated gene silencing, or position-effect variegation (Swenson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study that characterized Oddjob function in gene silencing.

claim: Knockdown or over-expression of Odj is lethal in D. melanogaster.
source: Knockdown or over-expression of Odj is lethal in D. melanogaster, although the functional basis for this lethality is still unknown (Schertel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study that reported Oddjob lethality phenotype.

claim: CG17802 was renamed as Nicknack (Nnk).
source: In keeping with the Oddjob nomenclature theme of 'James Bond henchmen,' and the mutant phenotype (described below), we renamed CG17802 as Nicknack, or Nnk.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the renaming of a gene.

claim: CG17801 knockdown in the germline led to de-repression of HetA and Blood transposable elements in the ovary.
source: Although previous studies found that the knockdown of CG17801 in the germline led to de-repression of HetA and Blood transposable elements in the ovary, CG17801 knockdown did not significantly impair fertility or viability (Czech et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study that characterized CG17801 function.

claim: CG17801 knockdown did not significantly impair fertility or viability.
source: Although previous studies found that the knockdown of CG17801 in the germline led to de-repression of HetA and Blood transposable elements in the ovary, CG17801 knockdown did not significantly impair fertility or viability (Czech et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study that characterized CG17801 phenotype.

claim: Ubiquitous knockdown of either Odj or Nnk greatly reduces adult viability.
source: Consistent with previous results (Schertel et al., 2015), we found that the ubiquitous knockdown of Odj or Nnk is lethal.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on knockdown phenotypes, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Knockdowns of CG17801, CG17803 and CG17806 are viable.
source: In contrast, we found that knockdowns of CG17801, CG17803 and CG17806 are viable (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on knockdown phenotypes, with reference to Figure 2B.

claim: Oddjob orthologs are present throughout 40 million years of Drosophila evolution.
source: Although Oddjob orthologs are present throughout 40 million years of Drosophila evolution, no other member of the D. melanogaster Odj-Nnk cluster is universally present in Drosophila species.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results.

claim: No other member of the D. melanogaster Odj-Nnk cluster is universally present in Drosophila species.
source: Although Oddjob orthologs are present throughout 40 million years of Drosophila evolution, no other member of the D. melanogaster Odj-Nnk cluster is universally present in Drosophila species.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results.

claim: CG17801 has been lost in the obscura group.
source: While CG17801 has been lost in the obscura group,CG17806 underwent multiple independent duplication and loss events.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: CG17806 underwent multiple independent duplication and loss events.
source: While CG17801 has been lost in the obscura group,CG17806 underwent multiple independent duplication and loss events.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: CG17803 arose in the ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. ananassae and underwent two independent losses.
source: CG17803 arose in the ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. ananassae and underwent two independent losses.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results.

claim: Nnk appears to have arisen in the ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. pseudoobscura (~30 mya).
source: Finally, Nnk appears to have arisen in the ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. pseudoobscura (~30 mya, Figure 1), and later experienced multiple independent duplications and losses (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results, with reference to Figures 1 and 2C.

claim: Nnk experienced multiple independent duplications and losses.
source: Finally, Nnk appears to have arisen in the ancestor of D. melanogaster and D. pseudoobscura (~30 mya, Figure 1), and later experienced multiple independent duplications and losses (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting phylogenomic analysis results, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Despite its essential function in D. melanogaster, Nnk is not universally conserved in Drosophila species.
source: Based on these analyses, we conclude that, despite its essential function in D. melanogaster, Nnk is not universally conserved in Drosophila species.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on phylogenomic analysis.

claim: The Nnk VDRC RNAi line does not have an insertion upstream of the tiptop gene.
source: We found that the Nnk VDRC RNAi line does not have an insertion upstream of the tiptop gene, which is associated with lethality in other KK lines (Green et al., 2014; Vissers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental validation of the RNAi line, citing previous studies about tiptop-associated lethality.

claim: Lethality from Nnk RNAi knockdown can be rescued via complementation with an intact Nnk-mel rescue transgene.
source: Second, we were able to rescue this lethality via complementation with an intact Nnk-mel rescue transgene.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental rescue results, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: The piggyBac insertion two bp upstream of the start codon in the 5' UTR of Nnk is homozygous lethal.
source: We found that this insertion allele is homozygous lethal but viability can be fully rescued upon mobilization of the piggyBac element, which repairs the intact 5' UTR in a 'scarless' fashion to restore Nnk function (schematized in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on the piggyBac-null allele phenotype, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Viability of piggyBac-null Nnk can be fully rescued upon mobilization of the piggyBac element.
source: We found that this insertion allele is homozygous lethal but viability can be fully rescued upon mobilization of the piggyBac element, which repairs the intact 5' UTR in a 'scarless' fashion to restore Nnk function (schematized in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental rescue results, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: piggyBac-null flies can be rescued by the Nnk-rescue transgene.
source: Furthermore, piggyBac-null flies can also be rescued by the Nnk-rescue transgene (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental rescue results, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The CRISPR-null Nnk allele is lethal when paired with a Nnk-spanning deficiency.
source: Contrary to previous results, we found that this allele is lethal when paired with a Nnk-spanning deficiency (BL9207, Figure 3D) and also fails to complement the piggyBac-null allele (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 1; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on the CRISPR-null allele phenotype, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The CRISPR-null Nnk allele fails to complement the piggyBac-null allele.
source: Contrary to previous results, we found that this allele is lethal when paired with a Nnk-spanning deficiency (BL9207, Figure 3D) and also fails to complement the piggyBac-null allele (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 1; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on complementation, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: The Nnk-rescue transgene can restore the viability of the CRISPR-null Nnk allele.
source: Moreover, the Nnk-rescue transgene can restore the viability of the CRISPR-null Nnk allele (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental rescue results, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Nnk is unambiguously an essential gene in D. melanogaster.
source: Based on all these results, we conclude that Nnk is unambiguously an essential gene in D. melanogaster.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Nnk-null progeny progress through embryogenesis at the same rate as their heterozygote siblings.
source: We found that Nnk-null progeny progress through embryogenesis at the same rate as their heterozygote siblings and are morphologically indistinguishable from heterozygotes until the L1 larval stage.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on developmental progression.

claim: Nnk-null progeny are morphologically indistinguishable from heterozygotes until the L1 larval stage.
source: We found that Nnk-null progeny progress through embryogenesis at the same rate as their heterozygote siblings and are morphologically indistinguishable from heterozygotes until the L1 larval stage.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on larval morphology.

claim: Nnk-null larvae are able to move toward and consume yeast paste much like their heterozygote siblings.
source: The Nnk-null larvae are able to move toward and consume yeast paste much like their heterozygote siblings.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on larval behavior.

claim: When heterozygote siblings molt into the L2 stage 48 hr AEL, Nnk-null larvae do not molt.
source: However, when heterozygote siblings molt into the L2 stage 48 hr after egg laying (AEL), Nnk-null larvae do not molt (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on larval molting, with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: 48 hr AEL, Nnk-null larvae progressively become unable to move or eat, eventually dying by 60 hr AEL.
source: Instead, 48 hr AEL, Nnk-null larvae progressively become unable to move or eat, eventually dying by 60 hr AEL.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on larval phenotype and lethality.

claim: Dietary supplementation with ecdysone precursor, cholesterol (7DH), or ecdysone (20E) cannot bypass or significantly delay the death of Nnk-null larvae.
source: We therefore, tested whether dietary supplementation with an ecdysone precursor, cholesterol (7DH, or 7-Dehydrocholesterol) or ecdysone (20E, or 20-Hydroxyecdysone) could bypass or significantly delay the death of Nnk-null larvae (Figure 4C). We found that it could not.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on dietary supplementation, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Dietary supplementation with cholesterol, 7DH, or 20E can significantly restore the viability of Npc1a larvae.
source: In contrast, the same dietary supplementation is able to significantly restore the viability of Npc1a larvae, which lack an essential transporter of cholesterol (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on dietary supplementation as a positive control, with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Nnk plays an essential role in larval progression in D. melanogaster that is distinct from known steps of the ecdysone biosynthesis pathway.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that Nnk plays an essential role in larval progression in D. melanogaster that is distinct from known steps of the ecdysone biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on dietary supplementation experiments.

claim: 249 genes (2.4% of all expressed genes) are differentially expressed between Nnk-null larvae and control larvae at 24 hr AEL.
source: At this timepoint, we find that 249 genes (2.4% of all expressed genes) are differentially expressed between Nnk-null larvae and control larvae, with 116 genes at least two-fold upregulated and 133 genes two-fold downregulated in Nnk-null larvae (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: 116 genes are at least two-fold upregulated in Nnk-null larvae at 24 hr AEL.
source: At this timepoint, we find that 249 genes (2.4% of all expressed genes) are differentially expressed between Nnk-null larvae and control larvae, with 116 genes at least two-fold upregulated and 133 genes two-fold downregulated in Nnk-null larvae (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: 133 genes are two-fold downregulated in Nnk-null larvae at 24 hr AEL.
source: At this timepoint, we find that 249 genes (2.4% of all expressed genes) are differentially expressed between Nnk-null larvae and control larvae, with 116 genes at least two-fold upregulated and 133 genes two-fold downregulated in Nnk-null larvae (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 4D.

claim: Among genes downregulated in Nnk-null L1 larvae, there is a significant over-representation of functional categories related to proteolysis and sterol transport.
source: Among genes downregulated in Nnk-null L1 larvae, we find a significant over-representation of functional categories related to proteolysis and sterol transport (both important functions during larval development), as well as dopamine monooxygenase activity (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting Gene Ontology enrichment analysis results.

claim: Genes related to lysosome, cytochrome P450s, and eye-related functions are upregulated upon Nnk loss at 24 hr AEL.
source: In contrast, we find that genes related to lysosome, cytochrome P450s (also important for larval molts), and eye-related functions are upregulated upon Nnk loss.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting Gene Ontology enrichment analysis results.

claim: 3027 genes (28.1% of all expressed genes) are differentially expressed between Nnk-null larvae and control larvae at 48 hr AEL.
source: At this timepoint, we find that 3027 (28.1% of all expressed genes) genes are differentially expressed, with 1301 genes at least two-fold upregulated and 1726 genes two-fold downregulated in the Nnk-null mutants compared to the age-matched controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: 1301 genes are at least two-fold upregulated in Nnk-null larvae at 48 hr AEL.
source: At this timepoint, we find that 3027 (28.1% of all expressed genes) genes are differentially expressed, with 1301 genes at least two-fold upregulated and 1726 genes two-fold downregulated in the Nnk-null mutants compared to the age-matched controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: 1726 genes are two-fold downregulated in Nnk-null larvae at 48 hr AEL.
source: At this timepoint, we find that 3027 (28.1% of all expressed genes) genes are differentially expressed, with 1301 genes at least two-fold upregulated and 1726 genes two-fold downregulated in the Nnk-null mutants compared to the age-matched controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Nnk-null larvae at 48 hr AEL are transcriptionally more similar to control larvae at 24 hr AEL than they are to age-matched control larvae.
source: Intriguingly, clustering samples by the transcriptional profile of all genes shows that Nnk-null larvae at 48 hr AEL are transcriptionally more similar to control larvae at 24 hr AEL of either genotype than they are to age-matched control larvae (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting clustering analysis results, with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Oddjob has a broad localization pattern within heterochromatin marked by H3K9me3.
source: Upon induction, we confirm that Oddjob has a broad localization pattern within heterochromatin (marked by histone H3 lysine nine methylation, H3K9me3 and outlined with a dashed line, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on protein localization, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The Nnk-encoded protein localizes to heterochromatin, but its localization is restricted to discrete foci, unlike Oddjob.
source: We found that the Nnk-encoded protein also localizes to heterochromatin, but its localization is restricted to discrete foci, unlike Oddjob (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on protein localization, with reference to Figure 5A.

claim: Constitutive pCopia-driven expression confirms the broad Odj and discrete Nnk localization within heterochromatin of D. melanogaster S2 cells.
source: These analyses also revealed a broad heterochromatic localization of Odj contrasting with discrete foci within heterochromatin for Nnk protein (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on protein localization using a different promoter, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Nnk foci do not overlap with centromeres (identified by the centromeric histone Cid).
source: These foci do not overlap with centromeres (identified by the centromeric histone Cid) or dual-strand piRNA clusters (marked by the piRNA-binding HP1 protein Rhino) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on protein localization relative to centromeres, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nnk foci do not overlap with dual-strand piRNA clusters (marked by the piRNA-binding HP1 protein Rhino).
source: These foci do not overlap with centromeres (identified by the centromeric histone Cid) or dual-strand piRNA clusters (marked by the piRNA-binding HP1 protein Rhino) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on protein localization relative to piRNA clusters, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ChIP-seq analyses confirms that Odj binding is highly enriched throughout heterochromatin.
source: Consistent with its cytological localization (Figure 5A and B), we found that Odj was highly enriched throughout the large chromosome regions previously defined as pericentric heterochromatin (Hoskins et al., 2015) whereas Nnk-bound regions are more narrowly distributed within heterochromatin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting ChIP-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 5C and a citation.

claim: Nnk-bound regions are more narrowly distributed within heterochromatin compared to Odj.
source: Consistent with its cytological localization (Figure 5A and B), we found that Odj was highly enriched throughout the large chromosome regions previously defined as pericentric heterochromatin (Hoskins et al., 2015) whereas Nnk-bound regions are more narrowly distributed within heterochromatin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting ChIP-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: Odj has two potential PxVxL motifs in the linker and ZNF domains.
source: Indeed, Odj has two potential PxVxL motifs, which are putative interaction sites for HP1a (Smothers and Henikoff, 2000), in the linker and ZNF domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting sequence analysis results, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and a citation.

claim: The PxVxL motif in the Odj linker domain is well-conserved across Drosophila species.
source: Investigating Odj orthologs in other Drosophila species revealed that the PxVxL motif in the linker domain is well-conserved, but the one in the ZNF domain is not.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting comparative sequence analysis results.

claim: The PxVxL motif in the Odj ZNF domain is not conserved across Drosophila species.
source: Investigating Odj orthologs in other Drosophila species revealed that the PxVxL motif in the linker domain is well-conserved, but the one in the ZNF domain is not.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting comparative sequence analysis results.

claim: Mutation of the putative HP1a-interaction site in the linker domain (V164A) converted Odj localization from a broad to a discrete pattern that at least partially overlapped with Nnk.
source: We found that mutation of the putative HP1a-interaction site in the linker domain (V164A) converted Odj localization from a broad to a discrete pattern that at least partially overlapped with Nnk (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on mutant protein localization, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mutation of the second putative PxVxL site (V321A) did not significantly affect Odj localization.
source: In contrast, mutation of the second putative PxVxL site (V321A) did not significantly affect Odj localization.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results on mutant protein localization.

claim: The putative PxVxL motif in the Odj linker region is a major contributor to Oddjob's broad localization to heterochromatin potentially by mediating a direct interaction with HP1a.
source: Our results suggest that the putative PxVxL motif in the Odj linker region is a major contributor to Oddjob's broad localization to heterochromatin potentially by mediating a direct interaction with HP1a.

claim: Nnk lacks a canonical PxVxL motif.
source: In the absence of this interaction, Oddjob and Nnk (which lacks a canonical PxVxL motif) localize similarly to discrete foci within heterochromatin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the context of explaining why Nnk localizes to discrete foci, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: In the absence of the PxVxL interaction, Oddjob and Nnk localize similarly to discrete foci within heterochromatin.
source: In the absence of this interaction, Oddjob and Nnk (which lacks a canonical PxVxL motif) localize similarly to discrete foci within heterochromatin (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental observations on protein localization, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: Some heterochromatin-embedded repetitive elements are derepressed upon Nnk loss.
source: Instead, we found that some heterochromatin-embedded repetitive elements are derepressed upon Nnk loss (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting RNA-seq analysis results, with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Both D. melanogaster and D. simulans Nnk proteins similarly localize to foci within heterochromatin in D. melanogaster S2 cells.
source: We found that both proteins similarly localize to foci within heterochromatin (Figure 6A–B; dashed line marks heterochromatin boundaries).

claim: The rapid evolution of Nnk during D. melanogaster- D. simulans divergence has not dramatically affected its gross subcellular localization.

evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on localization experiments.

claim: The Nnk-mel transgene significantly rescued Nnk knockdown compared to no-transgene controls.
source: We found that the Nnk-mel transgene significantly rescued Nnk knockdown compared to no-transgene controls; however, males were recovered at slightly lower levels than females (67 males: 101 females compared to expectation of 1:1 ratio; p=0.08, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental rescue results with statistical analysis.

claim: Males were recovered at slightly lower levels than females in Nnk-mel transgene rescue (67 males: 101 females, p=0.08).
source: We found that the Nnk-mel transgene significantly rescued Nnk knockdown compared to no-transgene controls; however, males were recovered at slightly lower levels than females (67 males: 101 females compared to expectation of 1:1 ratio; p=0.08, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results with statistical analysis.

claim: The D. simulans Nnk transgene can significantly rescue the lethality caused by knockdown of endogenous D. melanogaster Nnk in females.
source: We similarly found that the D. simulans Nnk transgene can significantly rescue the lethality caused by knockdown of endogenous D. melanogaster Nnk in females (Figure 6C), although at a slightly lower level than Nnk-mel rescue.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental rescue results, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Rescue of male viability by D. simulans Nnk is extremely poor (2 males: 33 females, p<0.0001).
source: In contrast, rescue of male viability by D. simulans Nnk is extremely poor (2 males: 33 females compared to expectation of 1:1 ratio; p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test) resulting in a severe sex-bias.
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting experimental results with statistical analysis.

claim: Nnk-sim is much worse than Nnk-mel in rescuing male viability (67:101 versus 2:33, p<0.0001).
source: Thus, Nnk-sim is much worse than Nnk-mel in rescuing male viability (67:101 versus 2:33, p<0.0001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting statistical comparison of rescue experiments.

claim: The D. simulans Nnk-rescue transgene specifically fails to rescue Nnk-knockout males, in the presence of the heterochromatin-rich Y chromosome.
source: Based on these findings, we infer that the D. simulans Nnk-rescue transgene specifically fails to rescue Nnk-knockout males, in the presence of the heterochromatin-rich Y chromosome.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on rescue experiments.

claim: Positive selection of Nnk is required for optimal function in the D. melanogaster genome.
source: Our findings suggest that not only is Nnk a positively-selected, essential ZAD-ZNF gene, but also that its positive selection is required for optimal function in the D. melanogaster genome.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on rescue experiments showing functional divergence.

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes arose in the ancestor of vertebrates and arthropods.
source: ZAD-ZNF genes arose in the ancestor of vertebrates and arthropods, but dramatically expanded within insect lineages (Chung et al., 2007), becoming the most abundant class of TFs in many genomes, including in D. melanogaster (Chung et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about ZAD-ZNF gene evolution.

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes dramatically expanded within insect lineages.
source: ZAD-ZNF genes arose in the ancestor of vertebrates and arthropods, but dramatically expanded within insect lineages (Chung et al., 2007), becoming the most abundant class of TFs in many genomes, including in D. melanogaster (Chung et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about ZAD-ZNF gene expansion.

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes are the most abundant class of TFs in many insect genomes, including in D. melanogaster.

claim: KZNF genes arose in the ancestor of tetrapods.

claim: KZNF genes expanded through lineage-specific gene amplifications to become the most abundant class of transcription factors present in mammalian genomes.
source: KZNF genes arose in the ancestor of tetrapods and expanded through lineage-specific gene amplifications to become the most abundant class of transcription factors present in mammalian genomes (Emerson and Thomas, 2009; Imbeault et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about KZNF gene expansion.

claim: Many KZNF genes play a critical role in genome defense through recognition and repression of transposable elements.
source: Many KZNF genes play a critical role in genome defense through recognition and repression of transposable elements (Wolf and Goff, 2009; Rowe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about KZNF gene function.

claim: KZNF genes involved in genome defense are subject to rapid genetic turnover and positive selection of their DNA-binding domains.
source: As a result, KZNF genes involved in genome defense are subject to rapid genetic turnover and positive selection of their DNA-binding domains (Thomas and Schneider, 2011).

source: Approximately half of all ZAD-ZNF genes are highly expressed in ovaries and early embryos (Chung et al., 2002), where they might play crucial roles for fertility or development.
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study about ZAD-ZNF gene expression patterns.

claim: 21 ZAD-ZNF proteins bind to unique DNA consensus sequences.
source: Biochemical characterization of 21 ZAD-ZNF proteins shows that they bind to unique DNA consensus sequences, with putative targets in the regulatory regions of specific target genes (Krystel and Ayyanathan, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study about ZAD-ZNF DNA-binding specificity.

claim: M1BP (Motif 1 Binding Protein) binds core promoters and promotes the expression of numerous housekeeping genes.
source: For example, the ZAD-ZNF protein M1BP (Motif 1 Binding Protein) binds core promoters and promotes the expression of numerous housekeeping genes (Baumann et al., 2017; Li and Gilmour, 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about M1BP function.

source: Similarly, ZAD-ZNF gene Grauzone promotes cortex expression and is necessary for meiotic progression during oogenesis (Chen et al., 2000; Harms et al., 2000; Page and Orr-Weaver, 1996).

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes Molting Defective, Ouija Board, and Séance encode proteins that promote the transcription of heterochromatin-embedded genes, Spookier and Neverland, required for larval progression.
source: Finally ZAD-ZNF genes Molting Defective, Ouija Board, and Séance encode proteins that promote the transcription of heterochromatin-embedded genes, Spookier and Neverland, required for larval progression (Uryu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study about these ZAD-ZNF genes' function.

source: Another ZAD-ZNF protein encoded by CG17801 helps repress HetA and Blood transposable elements in the ovary (Czech et al., 2013).

evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about these ZAD-ZNF proteins' function.

source: Even though the Weckle ZAD-ZNF protein possesses zinc-finger domains, it localizes to the plasma membrane instead of nuclear chromatin, where it interacts with the Toll-MyD88 complex to help establish the anterior-posterior axis of the developing embryo (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study about Weckle localization.

claim: Weckle interacts with the Toll-MyD88 complex to help establish the anterior-posterior axis of the developing embryo.
source: Even though the Weckle ZAD-ZNF protein possesses zinc-finger domains, it localizes to the plasma membrane instead of nuclear chromatin, where it interacts with the Toll-MyD88 complex to help establish the anterior-posterior axis of the developing embryo (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing a previous study about Weckle function.

claim: 30% of 185 evolutionarily young genes in D. melanogaster have acquired roles in development, cell biology, and reproduction that render them essential for viability or fertility.
source: However, recent studies demonstrated that 30% of 185 evolutionarily young genes in D. melanogaster (Chen et al., 2010) have acquired roles in development, cell biology, and reproduction that render them essential for viability or fertility (Lee et al., 2017; Long et al., 2013; Ross et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a direct statement citing previous studies about young essential genes.

claim: Nnk has undergone 52 fixed non-synonymous differences in the 439 aa protein-coding region during D. melanogaster-D. simulans divergence.
source: Nnk has also evolved under dramatic positive selection in just the 2.5 million-year divergence between D. melanogaster and D. simulans, having undergone 52 fixed non-synonymous differences in the 439 aa protein-coding region (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement reporting the number of fixed non-synonymous changes based on McDonald-Kreitman test results in Table 2.

claim: Altered protein–protein interactions or DNA-binding specificity via the linker domain may provide a means for functional diversification between closely-related ZAD-ZNF paralogs.
source: Our findings suggest that altered protein–protein interactions or DNA-binding specificity via the linker domain may provide a means for functional diversification between closely-related ZAD-ZNF paralogs.
evidence: This is a direct conclusion statement based on mutational analysis of Oddjob.

claim: Nnk may repress expression from heterochromatic repeats rather than acting as a transcription regulator for specific heterochromatin-embedded genes.
source: Based on these results, we hypothesize that rather than acting as a transcription regulator for specific heterochromatin-embedded genes like its paralogs Séance, Ouija Board and Molting Defective (Uryu et al., 2018), Nnk may instead repress expression from heterochromatic repeats.
evidence: This is a direct hypothesis statement based on RNA-seq and ChIP-seq results.

claim: Constant adaptation in ZAD-ZNF genes is driven by rapid alterations in heterochromatin across Drosophila and other insect species.
source: Based on our findings, we hypothesize that constant adaptation in ZAD-ZNF genes is driven by rapid alterations in heterochromatin across Drosophila and other insect species.
evidence: This is a direct hypothesis statement in the Discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: ZAD-ZNF diversification is driven by the high turnover of sequences embedded within heterochromatin.
source: Based on these observations, we propose that ZAD-ZNF diversification (marked by gene turnover and positive selection) is driven by the high turnover of sequences embedded within heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a direct proposal statement in the Discussion section based on the study's findings.

claim: The constant turnover of flanking and embedded sequence elements such as TEs and satellite DNAs may require constant adaptation of transcription factors required for the proper expression of genes embedded in heterochromatin.
source: We posit that the constant turnover of flanking and embedded sequence elements such as TEs and satellite DNAs may require constant adaptation of transcription factors required for the proper expression of genes embedded in heterochromatin.
evidence: This is a direct hypothesis statement in the Discussion section.

claim: ZAD-ZNF genes that are essential in one species could be lost in another because the target loci of the ZAD-ZNF genes is lost, or because another ZAD-ZNF paralog has acquired this essential regulation function.
source: Because of the high rate of evolutionary turnover of heterochromatic sequences, we hypothesize that ZAD-ZNF genes that are essential in one species could nevertheless be lost in another, either because the target loci of the ZAD-ZNF genes is lost, or because another ZAD-ZNF paralog has acquired this essential regulation function.
evidence: This is a direct hypothesis statement in the Discussion section.

claim: If the D. melanogaster Nnk protein, but not the D. simulans Nnk protein, could appropriately repress the D. melanogaster Y chromosome, this might explain the sex-bias seen in the D. simulans Nnk-rescue progeny.
source: For example, if the D. melanogaster Nnk protein, but not the D. simulans Nnk protein, could appropriately repress the D. melanogaster Y chromosome, this might explain the sex-bias seen in the D. simulans Nnk-rescue progeny.
evidence: This is a direct speculative statement in the Discussion section about the mechanism of sex-biased rescue.

claim: De-repression of the heterochromatin-rich Y chromosome could lead to detrimental consequences on larval development either directly or indirectly.
source: However, de-repression of the heterochromatin-rich Y chromosome could nevertheless lead to detrimental consequences on larval development. This effect could be direct, leading to inappropriate expression of Y-chromosome-embedded genetic elements that block larval development. Alternatively, this effect could be indirect; de-repression of the Y chromosome could indirectly impact several other chromatin processes genome-wide e.g., due to inappropriate titration of transcription or heterochromatin factors, which could exacerbate an already hypomorphic function of the D. simulans Nnk allele (Branco et al., 1869; Francisco and Lemos, 2014; Wang et al., 2018; Piergentili, 2010; Brown et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a direct speculative statement in the Discussion section about potential mechanisms, with citations to support the speculation.

claim: Different functional optimality of male-specific or female-specific Nnk functions could drive its rapid evolution.
source: Finally, different functional optimality of male-specific or female-specific Nnk functions could also drive its rapid evolution (VanKuren and Long, 2018).
evidence: This is a direct speculative statement in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: Rapid co-evolution with heterochromatic sequences might have driven the rapid evolution of Nnk and possibly other heterochromatin-interacting ZAD-ZNF proteins.
source: In any of these scenarios, we hypothesize that rapid co-evolution with heterochromatic sequences might have driven the rapid evolution of Nnk and possibly other heterochromatin-interacting ZAD-ZNF proteins.
evidence: This is a direct hypothesis statement in the Discussion section.
